statements.claim: Satadhanva fled on his mare Vijnatahridaya, which could carry him a hundred yojanas without rest, pursued by Krishna and Balarama seeking the Syamantaka jewel.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: Satadhanva's mare 'by name Vijnātāhridayā' could go over a distance of a hundred Yojanas, and with her he fled from Krishna; pack index: 'Krishna pursues and beheads Satadhanva near Mithila but finds no jewel'.

statements.claim: Satrajit was slain at night and the jewel Krishna had once bestowed on Satrajit was gone from his home.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'having slain Satrājit at the dead of night the highly powerful Shatadhanwā took away the jewel'; also 'the peerless jewel which Krishna conferred on Satrājit' — same source confirms Krishna had earlier given the gem to Satrajit.

statements.claim: Krishna and Balarama mounted their chariot and gave chase at once, determined to run the killer down before he could reach a friendly court.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata Purana 10.57.18: 'garuḍa-dhvajam āruhya rathaṃ rāma-janārdanau' — Rama and Janardana mounted the Garuda-bannered chariot in pursuit; Harivamsha: Satadhanva 'stricken with fear took to his heels' when Krishna returned.

statements.claim: After a hundred yojanas the mare failed in a grove on the approach to Mithila and stood motionless, her strength spent.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata Purana 10.57.19: 'mithilāyām upavane visṛjya patitaṃ hayam' — the fallen horse abandoned in a grove at Mithila; Harivamsha: 'Having travelled over a distance of a hundred Yojanas Shatadhanwa found her motionless'; Krishna speaks of 'the wretched plight of the mare'.

statements.claim: Krishna told Balarama to wait, went forward on foot with the discus, and struck down Satadhanva on the outskirts of Mithila.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: Krishna said 'Wait here... Going on foot I shall carry away the jewel Swyamantaka', then 'going on foot, Achyuta... killed Shatadhanwa on the way to Mithila'; Bhagavata 10.57.20 (padātis... tigma-neminā — on foot, with the sharp-rimmed discus) and pack summary: beheaded him with his discus.

statements.claim: Krishna searched the body and the fallen man's garments but found no jewel on Satadhanva.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57 summary: 'searching him found no jewel'; Harivamsha 1.39: 'Having slain the highly powerful Bhoja king he did not see Swyamantaka'.

statements.claim: Balarama demanded the jewel — 'Give me the jewel' — and when Krishna answered 'I have not got it', Balarama angrily cursed him, declared he would go away and have nothing more to do with him or the Vrishnis of Dwaraka.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.20-22): 'seeing Krishna return Balarāma said to him "Give me the jewel"'... 'Krishna said: "I have not got it." Thereat Rama was filled with anger. Repeatedly exclaiming "Fie on you, Fie on you"... "I forgive you because you are my brother. May you farewell. I go away. I have nothing to do with you or other Vrishnis of Dwārkā."'

statements.claim: Balarama entered Mithila, where King Janaka rose and received him with honor and gifts, and he stayed there for months, during which Duryodhana received from him instruction in the use of the mace.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.24-25: Janaka 'sahasotthāya' (rose suddenly) with pleased mind and honored him; 'uvāsa tasyāṃ katicin mithilāyāṃ samā' (stayed some months in Mithila); Harivamsha 1.39: 'the king Duryodhana received from Balabhadra the most excellent instructions in the use of clubs'.

statements.claim: Krishna returned to Dwaraka alone, the murderer punished and the jewel still lost.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.26: 'keśavo dvārakām etya' — Krishna returned to Dwaraka (Balarama having remained in Mithila); no jewel was found, per index summary.

notes: Every factual beat matches Bhagavata 10.57.9-25 and Harivamsha 1.39 (Dutt). Location phrasing harmonizes both sources ('grove on the approach to Mithila' / killed 'near Mithila'). 'Bent on avenging... and recovering the jewel', 'the same discus that had ended the lives of greater demons' and the closing suspense about the jewel's whereabouts are connective framing, not sourceable assertions.

statements.claim: The rains stopped when Akrura left Dwaraka and returned when he came back, as the Kukuras and Andhakas observed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.30-33): after Akrura's departure 'Pākashasana did not pour rain' and the country was devastated by drought; 'When the liberal Akrura returned to Dwārkā the thousand-eyed Indra began to discharge showers'; the Kukuras and Andhakas propitiated Akrura.

statements.claim: Krishna, returned from Mithila, saw that the slain Satadhanva received the funeral rites due to a kinsman.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata Purana 10.57.27: 'tataḥ sa kārayām āsa kriyā bandhor hatasya vai' — he caused the rites of the slain kinsman to be performed.

statements.claim: The night Satrajit was slain the jewel passed from Satadhanva into Akrura's keeping, bound by a vow that its hiding would never be revealed.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.35: 'nanu dāna-pate nyastas tvayy āste śatadhanvanā' (was it not deposited with you by Satadhanva?); Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.3-4): Satadhanva took the jewel 'and made a present of it to Akrura', who secured a promise that it would never be given out that the jewel was in Akrura's possession.

statements.claim: Akrura's own prosperity betrayed him: he gathered jewels and goods for a lavish sacrifice men called the Akrura Yajna and entered a vow of armor as though expecting danger.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39 (vv.24-27): Akrura 'entered into the initiation-like coat of mail for protecting himself', 'devoted most excellent jewels and various other articles to the performance of sacrifices', and 'that sacrifice... was called the Akrura Yajna'.

statements.claim: Before the assembly Krishna spoke to Akrura gently: was the jewel not entrusted to him by Satadhanva? Satrajit had no son, so the gem would pass to his daughter's sons, yet no one else could hold it — let Akrura show it to the kinsmen and bring peace to the house.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.35-38 near-verbatim: 'nanu dāna-pate nyastas tvayy āste śatadhanvanā / satrājito 'napatyatvād gṛhṇīyur duhituḥ sutāḥ / tathāpi durdharas tv anyais tvayy āstāṃ su-vrate maṇiḥ / darśayasva mahā-bhāga bandhūnāṃ śāntim āvaha'.

statements.claim: Akrura produced the Syamantaka; Krishna showed it to the assembled kinsmen, and the suspicion clinging to him since Satrajit's death dissolved.
statements.evidence: Bhagavata 10.57.39-40: Akrura, won over by these gentle words, showed the jewel 'syamantakaṃ darśayitvā jñātibhyo raja ātmanaḥ' (showing it to the kinsmen, [wiping] his own stain); Harivamsha: 'gave him the jewel in the midst of the assembled Satwatas'.

statements.claim: Krishna returned the jewel to Akrura, giving it up with a delighted heart.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'Hari, the repressor of enemies, returned it to him with a delighted heart'; Bhagavata index summary: 'then returned the jewel to Akrura'.

statements.claim: Balarama was brought home from Mithila by the car-warriors of the Vrishni race, Krishna among those who fetched him, and the brothers were reconciled.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'propitiating Balarāma all the mighty car warriors of the Vrishni race and the high-souled Krishna brought him back to the city of Dwārkā'.

statements.claim: Akrura, confirmed in Krishna's friendship, gave his own sister Sushila to Krishna in marriage.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.39: 'in order to please Krishna the intelligent Akrura gave him in marriage his sister Sushilā'.

notes: One nuance: the pack (Harivamsha) has Akrura extract the vow of secrecy FROM Satadhanva ('he made Shatadhanwā promise that he would never give out that the jewel was in his possession'), whereas the story's summary sentence has Akrura himself sworn to the fleeing thief; the substance — a pact of secrecy over Akrura's possession, kept until Krishna exposed it — is supported by both sources, so not counted as a contradiction. The rain motif, Akrura Yajna, assembly speech, jewel's return, and Sushila marriage are all directly grounded.

statements.claim: A wind bearing celestial fragrance blew over Dwaraka and flowers fell from a clear sky as the Yadavas sat at their daily business in the great assembly hall Dasharha.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.23-25): the assembly-hall 'celebrated by the name of Dāshārha' with huge golden door-ways, where 'the leading members of the Vrishni and Andhaka races, headed by Rāma and Krishna, used to carry on their daily transactions'; 'there blew the wind carrying celestial fragrance and there was a downpour of flowers'.

statements.claim: The king of the gods descended on his white elephant Airavata, the celestials gathered about him.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.26-27): 'Vāsava was seen, seated on a white elephant and encircled by the gods'; Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'ŚAKRA... came mounted on his fierce elephant Airávata to visit Śauri at Dwáraká'.

statements.claim: Rama and Krishna went out with King Ugrasena and the chiefs of the Vrishni and Andhaka houses to receive Indra, who embraced them in order of age and rank, entered the hall and accepted the offerings of hospitality.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.28-31): 'Rāma, Krishna and the king Ugrasena, with other leading Yādavas went out and welcomed the king of gods... the king of gods embraced Janārddana, Baladeva, the king Ahuka and then the other Yādavas, in order of age and rank... adored by Rāma and Krishna he entered into that magnificent assembly-hall... duly accepted arghya and other articles of hospitality'.

statements.claim: Indra touched Krishna's face with his hand — the auspicious countenance of his younger brother.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 v.32: 'Then touching the auspicious countenance of his younger brother (Krishna) with his hand the highly powerful Vāsudava addressed to him the following consoling words'.

statements.claim: Indra listed the oppressors Krishna had slain: Arishta, Dhenuka, Chanura, Mushtika, Kesin, Kamsa, Kuvalayapida, and the child-killer Putana, by whose fall the three worlds were preserved and the gods received their share of sacrifices.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'Arisht́a, Dhenuka, Cháńúra, Musht́ika, Keśin... have all been slain by thee. Kansa, Kuvalayápíd́a, the child-destroying Putaná, have been killed by thee... By thy valour and wisdom the three worlds have been preserved, and the gods, obtaining their share of the sacrifices... enjoy satisfaction'.

statements.claim: Naraka, son of the Earth and king of Pragjyotisha, had grown swollen with a boon granted by Brahma.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 v.34: 'Elated with the boon conferred on him by Brahmā the great Asura Naraka has foolishly stolen the ear-rings of Aditi'; Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'The son of the earth, called Naraka, who rules over the city of Prágjyotisha'.

statements.claim: Naraka had stolen Aditi's nectar-dripping earrings, Varuna's umbrella which no water can wet, and the jewel-crest of Mount Mandara; he had carried off 16,100 maidens of gods, saints, demons and kings, wearing a single braid, and shut them in a house on Mount Mani; and he now demanded Indra's elephant Airavata.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'He has taken away the umbrella of Varuńa, impermeable to water, the jewel mountain crest of Mandara, and the celestial nectar-dropping earrings of my mother Adití; and he now demands my elephant Airávata'; Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.12-14): 'sixteen thousand and one hundred chaste maidens, wearing a single braid of hairs, were brought... The powerful Bhouma made a house for them on the mount Mani'.

statements.claim: Naraka was unslayable by any creature but not by Krishna, and Garuda, capable of ranging anywhere and assuming any strength, would bear him to the demon's city.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.36-37): 'This Vinatā's son Guruda, highly powerful, capable of ranging anywhere and of assuming any strength... will take thee there. O Upendra, Bhumi's son, Naraka, is unslayable by all creatures. Do thou soon kill that sinful one and come back'.

statements.claim: Krishna smiled gently, rose from his throne, took Indra by the hand and thought of Garuda, who appeared; Krishna seated Satyabhama on his back, mounted behind her, and flew to Pragjyotisha.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'the divine Hari gently smiled, and, rising from his throne, took Indra by the hand: then wishing for the eater of the serpents, Garud́a immediately appeared; upon whom his master, having first seated Satyabhámá upon his back, ascended, and flew to Prágjyotisha'.

statements.claim: Razor-edged nooses defended the demon's walls, and four guardians — Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada, and Muru with his thousand sons — kept watch.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.120 (vv.18-19): 'He had four gate-keepers, dreadful in battle, namely Hayagriva, Nisunda, Panchanada and the great Asura Muru with his thousand sons'; Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'The environs of Prágjyotisha were defended by nooses, constructed by the demon Muru, the edges of which were as sharp as razors'.

statements.claim: Indra mounted Airavata and, in the sight of all Dwaraka, returned to the abode of the gods.
statements.evidence: Vishnu Purana 5.29: 'Indra mounted his elephant, and, in the sight of the inhabitants of Dwáraká, went to the abode of the gods'.

notes: Both sources (Harivamsha 1.120, VP 5.29) fully ground the episode. Minor spatial nuance: Harivamsha says the Dasharha hall itself 'extended over a yojana and had huge golden door-ways'; the story attaches the yojana dimension to its courtyard — cosmetic, not counted. Krishna's 'thought of Garuda' compresses VP's 'wishing for' Garuda. The maidens' number (16,100, single braid) and Mount Mani detail come from Harivamsha; the theft list from VP, as the pack notes.

statements.claim: Krishna came to Mount Raivataka with Rukmini for the festival closing the vow she had undertaken; his sons and brothers had been sent ahead by Narada's arrangement, and his sixteen thousand wives came in splendor befitting their rank.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.4-7): Krishna 'once went to the mount Raivataka with Rukshmini' because 'there was to take place a great festival on the day of the termination of Rukshmini's vow'; 'according to Narada's command, Vāsudeva's sons and brothers had already been sent there'; 'The sixteen thousand wives of the intelligent Madhava with splendour befitting their rank, had gone there'.

statements.claim: Krishna gratified the twice-born, beggars, those practicing religious rites and all who sought his well-being, and at the termination of the fasting honored Rukmini, daughter of Bhishmaka, before them all.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.8-11): 'the lord of subdued senses, conferred on the twice-borns all their desired-for objects, as well as on the beggars, on those who always practise religious rites and on all those who sought his well-being... At the termination of the fasting, the Lord highly honored his beloved spouse Rukshmini, the daughter of Bhishmaka'.

statements.claim: The ascetic Narada arrived while Krishna sat with Rukmini encircled by the other queens; Krishna received him with rites laid down in the scriptures, and Narada gave him a single Parijata flower.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.12-14): 'Krishna, sat on a seat with Rukshmini encircled by his other wives when the ascetic Nārada arrived... duly adored him with rites laid down in the Scriptures... Nārada... gave him a Pārijata flower'.

statements.claim: Because Rukmini sat beside him, Krishna gave her the flower; following his hint she set it in her hair and was doubly beautified by it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.15-17): 'Bhoja's daughter Rukshmini was by him, so Hari gave her that Parijata flower. Taking that lovely flower and following Krishna's hint, that blameless lady... put it on her head... was doubly beautified by that celestial flower'.

statements.claim: Narada described the flower's powers: it never withers; it gives wished-for fragrance for one year; heat and cold as desired and juices of every taste; whatever flowers she longs for; root of good luck and piety keeping the mind from evil paths; whatever color she wishes; thin or plump at her will; dispels unwholesome smell; serves as a lamp at night; garlands of Santanaka flowers and undecaying clothes; mastery over hunger, thirst and exhaustion; songs with musical instruments; and it leaves her when one full year is complete, the Creator having invested it with such a character.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.20-32) enumerates each power in the same order: never withers (20), wished-for fragrance for one year (21), heat/cold and juices (22), whatever flowers wished (24), root of good luck and piety, no evil path (25), color assumed, thin or plump (26), dispels unwholesome smell, lamp at night (27), Santanaka garland and undecaying clothes (28), mistress of hunger, thirst, exhaustion and decrepitude (29), songs with instruments (30), departs on completion of one full year (31), Creator's character (32).

statements.claim: Even the wives of the gods — Uma, Aditi, Sachi, Savitri and Sri herself — wear such flowers, and for them too the flower's stay lasts no more than a year.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.33-35): Uma (beloved spouse of Mahadeva, Himalaya's daughter), 'Aditi... Sachi, Savitri, the mother of gods and the goddess Sree too, always use this flower. Even for the wives of the gods and the leading celestial Vasus... its period of duration does not exceed more than a year'.

statements.claim: Narada declared Rukmini the foremost and most beloved among the sixteen thousand wives of Vasudeva.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 pack excerpt: 'among the sixteen thousand wives of Vāsudeva, I consider thee as the foremost and the most beloved.'

notes: The whole episode is a close rendering of Harivamsha 1.122 (Dutt). 'Mount Raivataka had never seen such a gathering' and the mood-shift of the closing lines are connective narration; the flower's powers, the one-year rule, the goddess list and Narada's declaration all track the source verse-by-verse.

statements.claim: Satyabhama's maids brought word-for-word news of the Raivataka festival: Krishna had come with Rukmini for the ceremony ending her vow, gratified the twice-born and others, and at the end of the fasting honored Rukmini, the daughter of Bhishmaka, before all his sixteen thousand wives.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.4-11): the same festival account (Krishna came with Rukshmini for the vow's termination, gratified twice-borns/beggars/rite-practitioners, sixteen thousand wives present, honored Rukshmini at the fasting's end), here recapitulated as the report that reaches Satyabhama.

statements.claim: Narada gave Krishna a single Parijata flower, which Krishna passed to Rukmini at his side; she set it in her hair, and the flower's powers included never withering, a year of wished-for fragrance, heat and cold at will, lamplight at night, any desired color, Santanaka garlands and undecaying clothes, and songs at a wish.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.14-16, 20-32): flower given to Krishna and passed to Rukshmini; Narada enumerates the same powers.

statements.claim: The goddesses of heaven — Sachi, Aditi, Savitri, Uma — wore such flowers, but even for them the flower's stay lasted no more than a year.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 (vv.33-35): Uma, Aditi, Puloma's daughter Sachi, Savitri, the mother of gods and Sree always use this flower; 'even for the wives of the gods... its period of duration does not exceed more than a year'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama, proud on the foundation of being the wife Krishna loved best, could not bear the accession of such good fortune to the other wife of her husband.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 pack excerpt: 'the highly proud Satyabhāma... could not bear the accession of such a good fortune unto the other wife of her husband.'

statements.claim: Worked up with anger like the flame of fire, Satyabhama cast off her ornaments where she stood and retired to the lonely apartment of anger, where she sat in the midst of her handmaids.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.122 pack excerpt: 'Worked up with anger like the flame of fire... she entered into the lonely apartment of anger'; Harivamsha 1.123 v.6 confirms she was 'inside the apartment of anger in the midst of her handmaids'.

notes: Fully grounded in Harivamsha 1.122-123. 'Rukmini... his first wife' compresses the source's 'beloved spouse' — acceptable as she is the wife honored at the festival. 'The room kept in the mansion for exactly such a mood, as if the palace itself expected this of its queens' and the closing suspense line are interpretive connective narration.

statements.claim: While Narada still sat with Rukmini praising the flower, Krishna noticed Satyabhama's absence and left the festival under some pretext.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 v.1: 'Finding the sage (Narada) seated with Rukshmini, the high-souled Keshava that knower of all things, set out under some pretext (for the mansion of Satyabhama)'.

statements.claim: Krishna went quickly toward the spacious mansion on the Raivataka hills that Vishvakarma himself had built for Satyabhama, walking slowly and with fear, aware that she, dearer to him than his own vital breaths, was under jealous resentment.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.2-4): 'the spacious mansion of Satyabhama that was built on the delightful Raivataka hills by Visvakarma himself'; 'he was aware that the daughter of Satrajit, his beloved queen—she dearer to him than his own vital breaths—had been under the influence of jealous resentment'; 'the slayer of Madhu proceeded with slow steps, and with greater fear'.

statements.claim: Krishna left Pradyumna to entertain and attend upon Narada, told his servant Daruka to wait at the gate, and entered the palace alone.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 v.5: 'Engaging Pradyumna to entertain and attend upon Narada and telling his servant Daruka "Wait at the gate," he entered into the palace of Satyabhama'.

statements.claim: From a distance Krishna watched her jealous gestures in the apartment of anger: sighing hot and frequently, a derisive laugh at a lotus nipped with her nails, figures drawn with her toe, deep thought with her face on her left palm, sandal smeared on her breast then cruelly thrown aside, and rising from and falling back into her bed.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.6-11): 'sighing hot and frequently'; 'laughing a derisive laugh mixed with sighs at the lotus... nipping with her nails'; 'describing figures on the ground with the tip of her toe slightly bent'; 'face resting on the lotus of her left palm'; 'take the delightful sandal from the hands of her maids, smear it on her breast and then again cruelly throw it aside'; 'rise from her bed and fall into it again and again'.

statements.claim: When she laid her head on her pillow with her veil over her face, Krishna, commanding the maids by signs not to announce him, approached with faltering steps, took up the fan and fanned slowly while laughing gently.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.12-14): 'as the daughter of Satrajit laid her head on her pillow, previously covering it with her veil, Janardanna thought "This is my opportunity"... by (manual) signs commanding the handmaids not to announce his presence, he approached Satyabhama with faltering steps. Taking up the fan and standing by her side, he then began to fan slowly and laugh gently'.

statements.claim: His contact with the Parijata flower perfumed him with a divine, supernatural, rare fragrance; Satyabhama uncovered her face and asked what it was, questioned her maids without glancing at him, and the maids knelt speechless with palms joined; she wondered whether the earth had emitted the scent, then her glance fell on Kesava.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.15-20): 'perfumed in consequence of his contact with the Pārijāta flower, diffused there a divine, super-natural and rare fragrance'; she 'uncovered her face, and said "What is this?"... without bestowing a glance on her godly husband, began to question her maids'; maids 'could not say anything, and kneeling down... with palms joined together'; she wondered if it were 'one of her excellent emissions' of the earth; 'her glance suddenly lighted on Kesava that creator of the worlds'.

statements.claim: She said 'Ah! right', her eyes dimmed with tears, pouting and sighing she turned her downcast countenance away, and with brows contracted in a frown and face on her palms told Hari, 'Thou lookest beautiful', as tears of jealous passion flowed like dew from lotus petals.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.21-24): "She said 'Ah! right,' and then suddenly her eyes became dimmed with tears... pouting and herself sighing... turned her down-cast countenance away... contracting her brows in a disapproving frown and placing her face on her palms, she said to Hari with her eyes upraised, 'Thou lookest beautiful'. Tears of jealous passion began to flow down from her eyes, like drops of dew falling from a pair of lotus-petals'."

statements.claim: Krishna approached in haste, held her tears in his hands, wiped the tears falling on her breast, and asked why tears flowed, why she wore plain white garments rather than those sprinkled with safflower and gold-dust, white being the dress of ladies worshipping the gods.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 (vv.25-30): 'approached her in haste and held them in her hands... wiping off with his hands those tears that were falling on her breast, that wearer of the mark of Srivatsa... spoke'; questions on tears (27), and garments 'sprinkled with safflower and gold-dust... white garments which ladies do not like to wear except at the time of worshipping the gods' (29-30).

statements.claim: Krishna protested: 'Just as flame is in fire, so my love resides in thee, and thee only.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.123 pack excerpt: 'Just as flame is in fire ... so my love resides in thee and thee only.'

notes: A faithful, nearly scene-by-scene rendering of Harivamsha 1.123 (Dutt). The commentary that he watched 'the theater of a woman who wanted to be angry at the one man she loved' is connective interpretation; all described gestures, the fragrance beat, the dialogue and the final protest are in the source passage.

statements.claim: Krishna entreated Satyabhama on his life to reveal the cause of her grief, saying her sorrow seemed to burn through all his limbs.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.1-3): 'sorrow seems to burn through all my limbs... I entreat thee, on my life, to reveal to me the cause of thy grief'.

statements.claim: Satyabhama spoke of her honor and prosperity established by Krishna in days gone by and famous in the world, and that being most beloved among his wives had prompted her pride.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.5-6): 'it was thy ownself that established my honor and prosperity... That I am most beloved of thee among all thy wives—is what prompted me to raise my head with pride above all others'.

statements.claim: She said her maids had told her she had been laughed at by her co-wives and others, that the Parijata flower Narada gave Krishna had been given to her dear one, totally neglecting her, an unmistakable expression of regard.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.7-9): 'to-day I have been laughed at by my rival (co-wives) and by other people... I hear that the Parijata flower that Nārada gave thee, thou hast given to thy dear one, totally neglecting my (poor) self... thou hast given unmistakable expression to—by presenting her with that best of all precious things'.

statements.claim: She accused: Narada eulogized her in Krishna's presence and he was gratified; if the sage had his reasons, why was the name of this unfortunate one uttered in that connection?
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.10-11): 'Narada also eulogised her in thy presence, and thou surely wert also gratified having heard that eulogy... why was it that the name of this unfortunate one was uttered in that connection?'

statements.claim: She said if she must repent for tasting the sweet liquor of his love she would rather have nothing to do with it, asked his permission, and declared she could not have believed even in a dream that he would honor another above her.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.12-13): 'if I am to repent for having tasted the (sweet) liquor of thy love, it is better I should have nothing to do with it? Be kindly pleased to accord me thy permission... I could not have believed even in my dream, that thou hast honored some body else more than myself'.

statements.claim: She charged that perhaps Narada had conceived a love for her rival but her grief was Krishna's presence in the scene, and that dishonored she no longer desired to live, her source of protection having become her source of fear.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.14-16): 'It may be that the sage Narada of incomparable powers has conceived a love for her (Rukshmini), but O lord, the cause of my grief in this, is thy presence in the scene... thus dishonored, I do not desire to live any longer. My source of protection has been turned to-day into my source of fear'.

statements.claim: She recalled his earlier assurance, 'O daughter of Satrajit, know that there is no wife of mine dearer to me than thyself', and asked what had become of it.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 v.22: 'Thou didst tell me in days gone by,—'O daughter of Satrajit, know that there is no wife of mine dearer to me than thyself'—What of that assurance! Or who cares to remember it!'

statements.claim: She called him a cheat and knave, fickle, deceiving and partial to her rival, claiming to have read his secret thoughts by his articulations and features, his tongue honeyed but too guileful.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.25-26): 'I did not know thee hence-before to be so much of a cheat and a knave; but now I have come to know thee as fickle, deceiving, and partial to my rival... I have read thy innermost and secret thoughts, O thief, by thy articulations and thy features and signs... it is thy tongue only that is honeyed, but thou art too guileful'.

statements.claim: Krishna consoled her, saying the sage Narada of unimpeachable deeds gave the flower to Rukmini out of generous feeling or regard for her to please Krishna — but he did not give it with his own hands.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 (vv.27-28 and passage): 'know me to be thine entirely... in order to please me the sage Narada of unimpeachable deeds gave that Parijata flower to her (Rukshmini) in my presence, merely out of generous feelings or regard for her; (but I did not give it with my own hands)'.

statements.claim: Krishna vowed: 'What to speak of a single flower — I shall fetch that best of all trees, the Parijata tree itself, from the gardens of paradise, and keep it in thy mansion... this shall be my foremost concern.'
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.124 pack excerpt: 'What to speak of a single flower, I shall fetch that best of all trees namely the Parijata tree itself, from the gardens of paradise, and keep it in thy mansion.'... 'so be it, then; this shall be my foremost concern.'

notes: Satyabhama's long speech and Krishna's consolation track Harivamsha 1.124 (Dutt) closely, nearly verbatim in places. The closing paragraph ('the whole tree it had come from, uprooted and planted in her own courtyard') is connective summary — the source promise is to fetch the tree and keep it in her mansion; no discrepancy counted.

statements.claim: Narada was preparing to take his leave when Krishna stopped him with an errand to heaven.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 v.1: 'finding that the sage Nārada was desirous of departing, spoke to him thus'.

statements.claim: Krishna asked Narada to go to heaven, interview the courtiers of the slayer of Tripura, and remind Pakasasana (Indra) of their ancient brotherly love, as a request, not a command.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.2-3): 'having repaired to heaven and there interviewed the courtiers of that intelligent slayer of Tripura... remind Pakasasana of all our ancient brotherly love that thou knowest—inform him not as my command but as my request'.

statements.claim: Krishna's message described the Parijata as the tree created by Kasyapa in days gone by for Aditi's happiness, bestowing religious merit and unbounded prosperity, given as a gift by the very virtuous goddesses in fulfillment of their vows; his wives, hearing of it, desired to give it away in turn for merit and for his gratification, so Indra should send it down to Dwaraka, to be restored to heaven after the ceremony of presentation.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.4-8): the Pārijāta tree 'which the illustrious and virtuous Kasyapa... created in days gone by for the sake of Aditi's happiness, that most excellent of all trees that bestows religious merit, and unbounded prosperity... given... by the very virtuous goddesses in fulfilment of their vows... my wives also hearing of the presentation of that tree, desire to give it away... Ask him therefore to send down to Dwarvati that best of all trees the Pārijāta; and it shall be restored to heaven after the ceremony of presentation is over'.

statements.claim: Krishna added that Narada should exert himself to persuade Indra, which would bring into prominence his ambassadorial abilities.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.9-10): 'thou shalt also so put forth thy endeavours that the lord of the immortals be persuaded to give over the excellent Parijata tree... this will also bring into prominence what ambassadorial abilities thou dost possess'.

statements.claim: Narada agreed to carry the message but said he was sure Indra would never part with the Parijata tree.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.11-12): 'Very well,—I shall thus speak to the lord of the gods... but I am sure he will never part with the Parijata tree'.

statements.claim: Narada recalled that the gods and Danavas had obtained the Parijata by churning the ocean with the Mandara mountain; the creator had wanted to take the tree away with Mandara, and Indra personally entreated Mahadeva, saying it was Sachi's sporting tree; Mahadeva granted the boon and did not bring the Parijata to the Mandara.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.13-17): 'The Danavas and the gods obtained this Parijata tree by throwing the Mandara mountain into the waters of the ocean... Sakra personally going to Sankara told him:—'This is Sachi's sporting tree, and may be allowed to remain in her gardens'... Mahadeva granted him the boon saying 'Let it be so then'... he did not also bring the Parijata tree to... the Mandara mountain'.

statements.claim: To please Uma, Hara created on the dales of the Mandara a self-luminous forest of Parijata trees extending over four miles, into which neither sun, moon nor wind could penetrate, where heat and cold reigned at the pleasure of the mountain's daughter; none could enter it but the god and goddess, their followers, and Narada himself; the Parijatas showered gems and jewels at a mere thought, and Shiva's attendants enjoyed the forest with his permission.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.18-23): 'Hara, in order to please his wife Umā, created on the dales of the Mandara mountain a forest of the Parijata trees extending over full four miles... neither the rays of the sun, nor the cool beams of the moon, nor even the breaths of the wind can penetrate... self-luminous, and heat and cold reign there at the pleasure of the mountain's daughter... Excepting the mighty god and goddess and their followers and myself... nobody... can enter that charming wood... the Pārijātas shower all kinds of best gems and jewels... as soon as they are merely thought of... troops of the illustrious attendants of Siva, also enjoy that beautiful forest'.

statements.claim: Narada told how the Daitya Andhaka, puffed up by a boon, transgressed into that forest and was slain by Hara, though ten times as powerful as Vritra and incapable of being slain by any created being.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.27-28): 'a mighty and dreadful Daitya of cruel motives by name Andhaka, who was puffed up with arrogance through the virtues of a boon... ventured to transgress into that forest... He was slain by... Hara, although he was ten times as powerful as Vritra and incapable of being slain by any created being'.

statements.claim: Narada concluded that the thousand-eyed Indra would never give the tree, obtained with such great difficulty, since it bestows all desires on Sachi and fulfills Indra's own wishes.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 (vv.29-30): 'the thousand eyed god Indra will never give thee, the Pārijāta tree obtained with great difficulty. That best of trees always bestows on the goddess Sachi all her desires, as well as... it fulfils the wishes of the highly powerful Indra'.

statements.claim: Krishna answered: if the lord of the immortals does not give the Parijata tree at Narada's request, he will hurl his mace at his breast.
statements.evidence: Harivamsha 1.125 pack excerpt: 'If that lord of the immortals do not give the Parijata tree at thy request, I shall then hurl my mace at his breast.'

notes: The entire message, Narada's recollection of the churning and of Shiva's Parijata forest on Mandara, the Andhaka anecdote, and the closing ultimatum are grounded in Harivamsha 1.125 (Dutt). 'As if the promise required the one thing no man could simply take' and the closing framing of plea-plus-warning are connective narration.
